name: valence_salience_listener

hypothesis: Listeners interpret referential expressions through an affective framing mechanism that scales object salience by the speaker's emotional valence. Under positive or neutral framing, feature-rich objects are perceived as desirable and salient targets, whereas under negative framing ('least favorite'), this preference is inverted toward plainer objects. The listener coordinates with the speaker by adopting this valence-modulated salience prior across both prior expectations and communicative inference.

name: literal_salience_listener
detail: ELPD-LOO -18655.1
hypothesis: Listeners interpret utterances literally rather than pragmatically: they select among referents of which the heard word is true based strictly on prior contextual salience, without simulating alternative words a speaker could have chosen. On a display with a one-feature object and a two-feature object that both possess the named feature, this mechanism predicts that listeners will favor the two-feature object because its greater feature count makes it more salient a priori, directly reversing the pragmatic model's prediction that the one-feature object is favored because a speaker meaning the two-feature object would have named its alternative feature.

name: costly_feature_speaker
detail: ELPD-LOO -18848.6
hypothesis: Speakers balance communicative informativeness against utterance production costs, incurring a penalty for producing shared, non-distinctive words that apply to multiple referents in the visual scene. Pragmatic listeners invert this cost-sensitive speaker, reasoning that an utterance describing a shared feature is less likely to have been chosen if a less costly distinctive alternative was available. On prior trials with no informative word, listeners choose uniformly among the available objects.

Under positive or neutral framing, feature-rich objects are perceived as desirable and salient targets, whereas under negative framing ('least favorite'), this preference is inverted toward plainer objects. The listener coordinates with the speaker by adopting this valence-modulated salience prior across both prior expectations and communicative inference.

name: rsa_l1_shared_prior
detail: elpd_diff 103.2 > 2.0 x clustered dse 22.9 vs parsimonious_literal_mixture (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Depth-1 RSA with the salience prior as common knowledge, used by the simulated literal listener as well as the pragmatic listener.

name: rsa_l1_salience
detail: elpd_diff 103.9 > 2.0 x clustered dse 22.9 vs parsimonious_literal_mixture (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Depth-1 RSA whose listener has a salience prior over objects (feature count, familiarization base rate) that the simulated literal listener lacks.

name: communicative_affordance_listener
detail: elpd_diff 149.3 > 2.0 x clustered dse 23.8 vs parsimonious_literal_mixture (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Listeners expect speakers to talk about objects that can be communicated effectively: before hearing an informative word, listeners assign higher prior probability to referents possessing greater communicative affordance, reasoning that a speaker constrained to a single word prefers to discuss topics that can be conveyed with high discriminative precision. In pragmatic reference games, listeners coordinate with the speaker on this topic prior, expecting the speaker's referential goal to favor objects with distinctive communicative descriptors over ambiguous ones.

name: rsa_l1
detail: elpd_diff 408.2 > 2.0 x clustered dse 72.9 vs parsimonious_literal_mixture (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Listeners invert a softmax-rational speaker who simulates a literal listener (depth 1), with a uniform prior over objects.

name: rsa_l2
detail: elpd_diff 408.6 > 2.0 x clustered dse 73.0 vs parsimonious_literal_mixture (grouped CV)
hypothesis: Listeners reason one level deeper (depth 2), inverting a speaker who simulates the depth-1 pragmatic listener.

name: costly_feature_speaker
detail: retired by the cap of 12 live models
hypothesis: Speakers balance communicative informativeness against utterance production costs, incurring a penalty for producing shared, non-distinctive words that apply to multiple referents in the visual scene. Pragmatic listeners invert this cost-sensitive speaker, reasoning that an utterance describing a shared feature is less likely to have been chosen if a less costly distinctive alternative was available. On prior trials with no informative word, listeners choose uniformly among the available objects.
